query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Differences in local chemical short‐range order, which alter the stacking fault energy and magnetic interactions, mediate the deformation mechanisms during tensile loading. In particular, the presence of Mn in the quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni introduces magnetic frustration that disrupts the formation of favorable SRO for nanotwinning and dislocation interactions, while its removal (as in the ternary CrCoNi and quaternary subsets) promotes a local atomic arrangement that lowers the stacking fault energy and enhances twin nucleation and dislocation mobility, leading to superior strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic single-phase FCC alloys of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, and their corresponding equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets produced by identical thermomechanical processing.
generation.intervention: Carry out identical in situ tensile deformation tests (at room temperature and controlled strain rates) combined with high-resolution electron microscopy (e.g., TEM complemented by atom probe tomography) on all samples.
generation.conditions: Samples processed to develop a single-phase FCC structure; deformations performed at ambient temperature under standardized strain rates to ensure a fair comparison of inherent mechanistic differences.
generation.structural_mediator: Variations in local chemical short‐range order that affect stacking fault energy and magnetic configurations, particularly influenced by the presence or absence of Mn.
generation.mechanism: In the quinary alloy, the chemical complexity with Mn leads to magnetic frustration and a less favorable SRO for promoting deformation twinning and optimal dislocation mobility. In contrast, in the ternary and quaternary subsets the reduction or removal of Mn enables a more ordered local atomic structure (lower stacking fault energy) that enhances nanotwinning and facilitates dislocation motion, thereby delaying strain localization and failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical testing conditions, the ternary (and to a lesser extent the quaternary) alloys will exhibit a higher density of deformation-induced twins and less dislocation pile-up, resulting in a combination of increased ultimate strength and ductility relative to the quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy processed to a single-phase FCC state under identical thermomechanical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to FCC single-phase alloys fabricated via identical thermomechanical processing and deformed at room temperature under controlled strain rates. It may not extend to alloys undergoing different processing methods or at extreme temperatures/strain rates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of local SRO and magnetic frustration to the mechanical properties remains to be fully determined. Variations in local composition and measurement sensitivity in detecting SRO may also introduce uncertainty in the magnitude of the predicted effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic samples of the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy and its quaternary and ternary subsets using identical thermomechanical processing to ensure a single-phase FCC microstructure. Perform in situ tensile testing at room temperature under controlled strain rates while monitoring deformation via high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography to characterize both the evolution of local chemical short‐range order and the associated twin/dislocation structures.
measurements: Local chemical short‐range order parameters (e.g., via atom probe tomography)
Stress–strain response (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ experiments reveal that the degree of local chemical short‐range order does not systematically differ between the quinary and lower constituent alloys, or if improved twin nucleation and the corresponding mechanical property enhancements (increased strength and ductility) are not observed in the ternary/quaternary alloys relative to the quinary baseline, then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractCrCoNi alloy exhibits a remarkable combination of strength and plastic deformation, even superior to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. We connect the magnetic and mechanical properties of CrCoNi, via a magnetically tunable phase transformation. While both alloys crystallize as single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solutions, we find a distinctly lower-energy phase in CrCoNi alloy with a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Comparing the magnetic configurations of CrCoNi with those of other equiatomic ternary derivatives of CrMnFeCoNi confirms that magnetically frustrated Mn eliminates the fcc-hcp energy difference. This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy, and is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries. This phase transformation sets CrCoNi apart from the parent quinary, and its other equiatomic ternary derivatives, and provides a new way for increasing strength without compromising plastic deformation. cited_evidence.text: We have shown the existence of a nanostructure with hcp phase in the equiatomic CrCoNi—an alloy widely considered to have a single-phase fcc structure. We observed a delineation between CrCoNi—with hcp as the ground state independent of the local atomic arrangements—and the CrCoMnFeNi HEA, where the magnetic frustration resulting from the addition of Mn breaks a clear trend for relative hcp vs fcc energies. In addition, we showed that there is no driving force for this phase transformation in any other equiatomic ternary derivatives of this HEA. These findings emphasize the fact that high-entropy alloys with more constituent elements are not necessarily superior to their derivatives. Instead, the combination of chemical and, as emphasized presently, magnetic identities of elements govern the properties. An important consequence of this finding is that new alloying combinations can be predicted based on similar favorable magnetic properties. These results provide a new paradigm for design of single-phase alloys with metastable structures through computational guidance and experimental validation.

Here, we perform hybrid MC/MD simulations to explore the effect of SRO on the mechanical properties of an equiatomic CoCuFeNiPd HEA. Monte Carlo is employed to exchange atoms of different types to lower the alloy energy by optimizing SRO, and MD is employed to both relax the local atomic structure/displacements and to simulate tensile deformation. The Warren-Cowley parameters (WCPs) for all elemental pairs are used to describe SRO. Our MC/MD simulations show that the SRO development in the CoCuFeNiPd HEA is energetically favored, which is also validated by DFT calculations. This SRO is characterized by a wide range of local environments/atomic-scale configurations. Our MD tensile deformation simulations in this HEA with and without SRO indicate that the SRO enhances both the ultimate strength and ductility of the HEA. The underlying deformation mechanism is phase transformation prior to the ultimate tensile stress and dislocation slip posterior to the ultimate tensile stress. We explore the strain-induced phase transformations by investigating the local relative stability of FCC and BCC structures (sensitive to the local elemental concentration). chosen.why: This approach directly tackles the open question by comparing the quinary alloy with its quaternary and ternary subsets under rigorously controlled conditions. It tests the mechanistic hypothesis that differences in local chemical short‐range order, not merely constituent count, drive the observed differences in deformation and failure. The use of standard in situ experimental techniques allows for direct measurement of dislocation behavior and potential activation of deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning, planar slip) that can either validate or falsify the hypothesis.
